lesson.title: Check the facts
lesson.subtitle: Spot made-up facts, and check before you share

video.title: Check the facts
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma marks a student’s project at her desk. A neat bar chart says 73% of homes have running water, with a footnote: “from a government report”. She searches for the report on her phone: nothing. She puts the pen down.
scenes.animation: The footnote highlights (150 ms); the phone search spins, then shows an empty result. Push-in on Salma’s face.
scenes.narration: A student’s project had a lovely number in it. Seventy-three percent of homes in our town have running water, “from a government report”. I asked to see the report. It doesn’t exist: a chatbot made it up.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name, the lesson title and the yellow AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: why AI sometimes makes things up, and how to check.

scenes.visual: The chatbot box writes a sentence, one piece at a time. It reaches a gap it knows nothing about, and without pausing fills it with a smooth, invented phrase.
scenes.animation: Words drop in steadily; the gap fills with no hesitation; a small warning icon blinks once.
scenes.narration: Remember how a chatbot writes: it predicts what’s likely, it doesn’t check what’s true. When it doesn’t know, it rarely says so. It fills the gap with something that sounds right. Even chatbots that search the web can mix up what they find.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI chip. Three invented things float out of the chatbot box: a number, a quote in speech marks, and a book with a question mark on its cover.
scenes.animation: Each card floats out in turn (300 ms apart) and gets a red outline.
scenes.narration: When AI states something false as if it were true, we call it a hallucination. It can invent facts, numbers and dates, quotes nobody said, and sources that don’t exist: books, links, reports.

scenes.visual: An AI answer on a phone with a highlighter moving through it, marking a number, a date, a name, a quote, and a line about the student’s own country.
scenes.animation: The highlighter sweeps each item in turn (250 ms).
scenes.narration: You can’t check every word, so check what matters. Exact numbers, dates and names. Quotes and sources. Anything about your own country, where it learned less. And anything you’ll hand in or share.

scenes.visual: A classroom: one student’s hand shoots up first every time, with a confident grin. Another student nods, then quietly opens the textbook to check before writing in her notes.
scenes.animation: The hand shoots up twice (150 ms); the textbook flips open.
scenes.on_screen_text: Like a classmate who’s always sure
scenes.narration: It’s like a classmate who always answers first and always sounds sure. They’re often right. But before you copy their answer into your notes for the exam, you’d check it in the book.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up a history project with a date circled in red. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A chatbot gives you a date for your history project. What should you do with it?

scenes.visual: The first card gets a check badge. The date is checked against an open textbook and a teacher’s nod; a chatbot asked twice gives the same wrong date twice.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); two ticks appear beside the date.
scenes.narration: Check it in two trusted sources. Your textbook, your teacher, or a trusted website, like a ministry, a university or a well-known news site. Asking the chatbot again isn’t checking: it can repeat its mistake just as confidently. Two sources that agree, and don’t just copy each other, are worth far more than one.

scenes.visual: A family chat on a phone: a dramatic flood photo, and a video of a famous footballer. Small labels slide over them: ‘Made by AI?’. A finger hovers over Share, then pulls back.
scenes.animation: Images pop into the chat (150 ms); the finger pauses over Share for 1 s, then moves away.
scenes.narration: It’s not only text. AI can make photos, videos and voices that look and sound real: a flood that never happened, a famous footballer saying something he never said. Before you share, ask: who made this, where’s the original, and do trusted sources report it?

scenes.visual: A phone shows the lab: an AI answer about the river Nile with three underlined claims. A finger taps one and picks a label: correct, wrong, or check a source.
scenes.animation: Each claim highlights in turn; the label buttons pop up under it.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: check the AI’s answer
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll check an AI answer about the river Nile, claim by claim. Mark each one correct, wrong, or check a source. One claim is a confident mistake, and one is completely invented.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone: a class group with a new video and a red ‘shocking!’ caption. Answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A shocking video of a famous person lands in your class group. What do you do first?

scenes.visual: The ‘Check before you share it’ card gets the check badge, then four summary lines tick in under ‘Remember’.
scenes.animation: Lines appear one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: Invented facts · Two sources · Check before sharing
scenes.narration: Check before you share: videos can be made by AI too. Remember: AI can invent facts, numbers, quotes and sources. Check what matters in two trusted sources. And if you can’t find it anywhere trusted, don’t use it.

scenes.visual: A student at a kitchen table with a textbook and a phone showing a forwarded message. Three facts are underlined; two get ticks, one gets a question mark. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Underlines draw themselves; ticks pop one by one; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: take an AI answer, or a message forwarded in your family group. Pick three facts from it. Check each one in your textbook, or with a teacher. How many held up? If one didn’t, tell the person who sent it, kindly.

checkpoints.prompt: A chatbot gives you a date for your history project. What should you do with it?

options.text: Check it in two trusted sources
Ask the chatbot if it’s sure

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — check it in two trusted sources, like your textbook and your teacher. Asking the same chatbot again isn’t checking.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a chatbot can repeat its mistake just as confidently, and sounding sure proves nothing. Check two trusted sources.

checkpoints.prompt: A shocking video of a famous person lands in your class group. What do you do first?

options.text: Share it fast to warn people
Trust it: videos can’t be faked

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — AI can make or change videos. Check who made it and whether trusted sources report it, then decide.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — AI can make videos that look real, and sharing fast spreads fakes. Check first, then decide.
